works.name: Cologne Cathedral
works.style: High Gothic, completed by the nineteenth century
works.tagline: Begun in 1248, abandoned in 1560 with a crane left standing on the unfinished tower, and finished 320 years later from the rediscovered medieval drawings.
history: In 1164 the archbishop of Cologne carried off from Milan the relics said to be those of the Three Kings. They made the city one of the great pilgrimage destinations of Europe, and they needed a setting. In 1248 the old cathedral conveniently burned down, and the chapter began a replacement modelled on Amiens — but bigger.

The choir was consecrated in 1322. Work then slowed, and around 1560 it stopped entirely, out of money and out of interest. For three hundred years the cathedral stood as a torso: a finished choir with a temporary wall, a nave a few metres high, and the south tower stopped at sixty metres with a wooden crane still standing on top of it. The crane became a symbol of the city.

Then, in 1814 and 1816, the original medieval elevation drawings for the west front were found — one half in Paris, the other in Darmstadt. Their rediscovery, at the height of German Romantic nationalism, turned finishing the cathedral into a national project supported by Protestant Prussia as much as Catholic Cologne. Building resumed in 1842, and on 15 October 1880 the cathedral was completed to the medieval design, 632 years after it was begun. It was then the tallest building in the world.

In the Second World War the city around it was flattened and the cathedral was hit by fourteen aerial bombs. It stayed up. Photographs of the twin spires standing over a field of rubble are among the most reproduced images of the war.
architecture: Because it was finished from the original drawings, Cologne is the most complete statement of French High Gothic ever built — more thoroughly Gothic than any actual French cathedral, since none of them was ever finished exactly as drawn. It is Amiens taken further: a five-aisled nave, a vault 43.35 metres up, and a west front of 7,000 square metres, the largest of any church.

The nineteenth-century builders were faithful to the design and unfaithful to the technique — where medieval masons would have used timber and iron cramps, they used steel roof trusses and cast-iron where it helped. The result is a medieval building with a Victorian skeleton in places, which is one reason it survived fourteen bombs.

Inside, the choir keeps its original glory: 104 oak choir stalls of about 1310, the largest medieval set in Germany, and the Shrine of the Three Kings — a gilded, jewelled basilica in miniature made by Nicholas of Verdun between 1180 and 1225, and the largest reliquary in the western world. In the south transept, Gerhard Richter's window of 2007 fills the tracery with 11,500 squares of coloured glass in an order generated by chance — a modern answer to a medieval question about light.

works.name: Palace of Westminster
works.tagline: A classical building wearing medieval clothes, designed by two men who disagreed about almost everything except the result.
history: On 16 October 1834 two workmen were told to burn a large quantity of obsolete wooden tally sticks — the Exchequer's old accounting system — in the furnaces under the House of Lords. The flues overheated, and the medieval palace of Westminster burned down overnight. Turner painted it from a boat.

The competition for the replacement required a design in the Gothic or Elizabethan style — a deliberate choice, asserting a native English constitutional tradition against the classicism associated with revolutionary France and America. Charles Barry won, in partnership with Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin, who was twenty-three and the most gifted Gothic draughtsman alive.

Both men were destroyed by it. Pugin, who drew essentially every detail, from the towers to the inkstands, collapsed into insanity and died in 1852 at forty. Barry died in 1860, the work unfinished; his son completed it in 1876. In May 1941 the Commons chamber was destroyed by incendiary bombs and was rebuilt to a plainer design after the war.
architecture: Barry's plan is rigorously classical — symmetrical, axial, organised around a central lobby with the Lords at one end and the Commons at the other, and a processional route running from the sovereign's entrance to the throne. On top of that logic Pugin laid a skin of Perpendicular Gothic, the fifteenth-century English style, worked in Anston limestone.

The asymmetry of the two towers rescues it. Barry's plan gave a flat 265-metre river front, which needed breaking; the Victoria Tower at one end, square and massive, and the clock tower at the other, slender and vertical, hold the composition between them like bookends.

Pugin's interiors are the argument made visible. He believed, and wrote in The True Principles of Pointed or Christian Architecture, that ornament must arise from construction and never be applied to disguise it, and that a building's character follows the morals of the society that raises it. Every tile, wallpaper, hinge, bench and stained-glass panel here was designed on that principle. The one medieval survivor of the fire, Westminster Hall of 1097, still stands beside it, carrying the hammerbeam roof put on for Richard II in the 1390s — the largest medieval timber roof in northern Europe, spanning 20.7 metres with no central support.

facts.v: Charles Barry with A. W. N. Pugin

look: A symmetrical classical plan hidden under Perpendicular detailing
The two mismatched towers holding a very long façade together
Pugin's ornament: everything from tiles to inkstands, all one hand

works.name: Neuschwanstein Castle
works.tagline: A castle designed by a theatre set-painter for a king who wanted to live inside an opera, and who died seven weeks before the public was let in.
history: Ludwig II of Bavaria became king at eighteen, lost his kingdom's independence to Prussia at twenty, and thereafter withdrew into building. Neuschwanstein was begun in 1869 on a crag above his father's castle at Hohenschwangau, and was meant, in his words, as a worthy temple for Richard Wagner, whose operas he had been financing since he was nineteen.

The first designs were not by an architect but by Christian Jank, a stage designer, who drew the silhouette; the architects Eduard Riedel and Georg von Dollmann then had to work out how to build it. Ludwig involved himself in every detail and every delay, and the costs ran to more than twice the estimate — paid from his private fortune and borrowed money, not from state funds, though his debts eventually became a state problem.

In June 1886 a government commission declared him insane — on evidence that has been questioned ever since — and deposed him. Three days later he was found dead in shallow water at Lake Starnberg with his psychiatrist beside him; no satisfactory explanation has ever been given. He had lived in the castle for a total of about 172 days. Seven weeks after his death it was opened to paying visitors, to recover the debts. Some 1.4 million people a year now come.
architecture: It is Romanesque Revival on the outside — round arches, a great keep, a gatehouse in red brick — but the plan is a nineteenth-century idea of a medieval castle rather than a copy of one, arranged for effect from a distance. Almost nothing about it is defensive. It is scenery, and superb scenery, sited so that it appears from the valley to grow out of the rock.

Behind the medieval face is the most advanced technology money could buy: a steel frame in parts of the structure, central hot-air heating, running water on every floor, flushing lavatories, an electric bell system for servants, and a telephone line.

The interiors are opera sets. The Throne Hall is a Byzantine basilica in gold mosaic with a two-tonne chandelier and a marble floor of two million pieces — and no throne, because it was never delivered. The Singers' Hall on the fourth floor copies the hall at the Wartburg where the medieval song contest of Tannhäuser was set. There is a grotto with an artificial waterfall between rooms. And it was never finished: only about fifteen rooms of the sixty-odd planned were completed. In 2025 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list along with three of Ludwig's other palaces.

facts.v: Christian Jank, a theatre set painter
Seven weeks after his death, in 1886

works.name: Sagrada Família
works.tagline: A cathedral being built out of geometry rather than precedent — and its architect's answer, when told it was slow, was that his client was not in a hurry.
history: The Expiatory Temple of the Holy Family was founded in 1882 as a conventional neo-Gothic church, funded entirely by donations. Within a year the original architect resigned and the commission passed to Antoni Gaudí, then thirty-one. He redesigned it completely and spent the last forty-three years of his life on it, the final fifteen exclusively, living on site in the workshop.

In 1926 he was knocked down by a tram on the Gran Via. Shabbily dressed and carrying no papers, he was taken for a beggar and left in a pauper's ward; he was recognised the next day, and died three days later. He is buried in the crypt of the building.

Ten years on, anarchists burned the workshop in the Spanish Civil War, destroying most of his drawings and smashing his plaster models. The models were painstakingly reassembled from fragments over decades — which is why the building's development has been so slow and so contested. Construction has run on donations and ticket money ever since. The nave was completed and the church consecrated as a basilica in 2010; the central Tower of Jesus Christ, which will make it the tallest church in the world at about 172.5 metres, is topping out for the Gaudí centenary in 2026.
architecture: Gaudí's structural method was to let gravity do the design. He hung chains from a board with weighted bags representing loads, photographed the result, and turned the photograph upside down — a hanging chain finds the line of pure tension, so inverted it becomes a line of pure compression. Build along those lines and the structure needs no buttresses at all. He called flying buttresses crutches.

The forms are ruled surfaces — hyperboloids, paraboloids, helicoids, conoids — shapes that curve but can be generated by straight lines, which means they can be cut, cast and now machined. The columns branch like trees to catch the vault at the angle the load wants; the hyperboloid openings in the vault let light down as though through a canopy. It is Gothic's logic, arrived at independently from first principles.

The three façades tell one story in three tempers. The Nativity front, the only one substantially built in Gaudí's lifetime, boils over with plants and animals cast from life. The Passion front, carved by Josep Maria Subirachs from 1987, is deliberately harsh, angular and stripped. The Glory front is still to come. Inside, the glass shifts from cool blues and greens on the east to reds and golds on the west, so the colour of the room changes across the day.

facts.v: Hanging chain models, inverted into compression
About 172.5 m — will be the tallest church

look: Columns that branch like trees, angled to meet the load exactly
Hyperboloid openings dropping light through the vault like a canopy
Nativity façade cast from real plants, animals and people
East windows cool, west windows hot — the room changes colour all day

works.name: Grundtvig's Church
works.tagline: Six million yellow bricks and nothing else: a west front built like the pipes of an organ, by a father and finished by his son.
history: A competition was held in 1913 for a church commemorating N. F. S. Grundtvig, the pastor, poet and educational reformer who shaped modern Danish national culture. Peder Vilhelm Jensen-Klint won it with a design that ignored every current fashion.

Building began in 1921 and went slowly, partly by design — the bricklaying was done to the highest possible standard by craftsmen paid to take their time, as a deliberate revival of the trade. Jensen-Klint died in 1930; his son Kaare Klint, later the founder of modern Danish furniture design, completed the work in 1940.

The church stands at the centre of a small district of housing also designed by the Klints, in the same brick and the same idiom, so the building sits in a setting made for it rather than dropped into a street.
architecture: Jensen-Klint studied the ordinary village churches of Denmark — plain, gabled, unornamented brick — and scaled their language up to cathedral size without adding anything to it. There is no stone, no plaster, no paint, no applied ornament anywhere. Roughly six million yellow bricks, all of one standard type, laid by hand.

The west front is the famous image: a stepped gable pulled up into vertical ribs of ascending height, so the whole 49-metre façade reads unmistakably as the pipes of an organ — appropriate for a man remembered above all for writing hymns. It is Gothic verticality expressed with no arch, no tracery and no carving.

Inside, the proportions are pure Gothic — a tall nave with aisles, ribbed vaults, pointed arcades — but everything is executed in the same yellow brick, including the vault ribs and the piers, so the interior is a single continuous material lit by clear glass. The effect is severe and startlingly warm at once, and the acoustic is famous; the church is used as a recording venue as much as a place of worship.

49 m to the top of the west gable
N. F. S. Grundtvig, hymn-writer and reformer

works.name: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral
works.tagline: A cathedral in the round, built in five years on the crypt of an abandoned scheme that would have been the second largest church on earth.
history: Liverpool's Catholic community — largely Irish, largely poor — had wanted a cathedral since the 1850s. In 1930 Edwin Lutyens designed one: a colossal domed basilica that would have been the second largest church in the world, with a dome wider than St Peter's. Work began in 1933 and stopped in 1941 with the crypt built and the war on. By 1958 the estimated cost had risen tenfold, and it was abandoned.

A competition in 1959 asked for something buildable on the existing crypt within £1 million and five years, seating 2,000 with the congregation gathered around the altar rather than strung out in front of it — a requirement that anticipated the reforms of the Second Vatican Council by several years.

Frederick Gibberd won against nearly three hundred entries. The cathedral was consecrated on Pentecost 1967. Construction defects in the aluminium cladding and mosaic led to a lawsuit and long repairs; local nicknames — Paddy's Wigwam, the Mersey Funnel — attached themselves permanently and affectionately.
architecture: The plan is a circle, 59 metres across, with the altar at the centre and the congregation on all sides, none of them more than about twenty metres away. That single decision does away with nave, aisles, choir and sanctuary — the entire spatial grammar of two thousand years of church building — and replaces it with a room.

Sixteen concrete trusses spring from a ring beam and lean in to carry a lantern tower, with the roof between them. The lantern is the whole light source: a drum of stained glass by John Piper and Patrick Reyntiens in blue, yellow and red, arranged so the colour falls and moves across the floor as the sun goes round. Chapels are set into the perimeter between the buttresses, each lit differently.

Underneath it all is Lutyens' crypt — vast Roman brick vaults from the 1930s, built for a building that never came, and now the strangest basement in England. The two cathedrals of Liverpool stand at either end of Hope Street: this one, and Giles Gilbert Scott's enormous Gothic Revival Anglican cathedral, begun in 1904 and finished in 1978. A city with two cathedrals, seventy years and a whole century of taste apart.

facts.v: Circular, 59 m across, altar at the centre
Lutyens' 1930s crypt for an abandoned cathedral
About 2,000, all within 20 m of the altar
